topics.title: What If You Controlled Everyone's Attention?
topics.premise: What if you could move 100% of a room's attention onto any person you chose?
topics.world: A livestreamed international talent final, where spotlights, applause, rankings and millions of remote viewers make attention visible and consequential.

thumbnail.image: You aim a battered remote as an entire audience turns toward one stunned performer beneath a glowing 100%.

topics.rule: Point at one visible person and transfer up to 100% of the surrounding attention to them. Attention cannot create approval or talent, only scrutiny. Every minute at 100% makes the remote's range expand.
topics.hook: Your best friend sings while everyone checks their phones—then you press one button, 1% becomes 100%, and every head snaps toward her.
beats: Your own introduction receives 0%, proving the remote measures real attention rather than politeness.
You give your terrified friend 100%; she finds her voice and wins the room.
Her score follows her backstage, turning one performance into instant status.
Consequence jump one: concentrated scrutiny makes her choke during a harder song and blame you.
You hide by placing 100% on a rival while changing the stage in plain sight.
The rival gets every eye but no affection, separating visibility from belonging.
Consequence jump two: contestants steal the remote and trade attention like a weapon.
You can keep 100% for your final solo or return it to the friend whose confidence you damaged.
You surrender your spotlight; the audience joins her chorus and she wins.
Consequence jump three: the display stops showing 100% and reads 2,400,000 VIEWERS—the livestream is now inside the remote's range.
restarts: Your friend's triumph becomes a choking hazard.
The rival proves attention is not affection.
The power expands from one auditorium to millions of screens.

content_mine.fact: People systematically overestimate how much others notice their appearance and mistakes, known as the spotlight effect.
content_mine.beat: Your embarrassing entrance feels enormous even though the remote reads 0%.

content_mine.fact: Another person's gaze can redirect attention even when gaze direction predicts nothing useful.
content_mine.beat: The first click produces a wave of turning heads.

content_mine.fact: Direct eye contact can increase arousal and self-awareness.
content_mine.beat: Your friend's posture changes when the entire room looks directly at her.

content_mine.fact: An audience can improve well-learned actions while impairing difficult or unfamiliar ones.
content_mine.beat: A rehearsed chorus succeeds, but a new arrangement collapses.

content_mine.fact: A large meta-analysis confirmed that task difficulty changes whether observers help or hurt performance.
content_mine.beat: You discover that 100% attention is useful only at the right moment.

content_mine.fact: Pressure and self-conscious monitoring can disrupt practiced performance.
content_mine.beat: Your friend consciously controls every note and freezes.

content_mine.fact: Social impact increases with the strength, immediacy and number of observers.
content_mine.beat: The power becomes overwhelming when it reaches the packed final.

content_mine.fact: Increasing the number of people staring upward caused progressively more passersby to stop and look.
content_mine.beat: A few redirected spectators organically recruit the rest of the crowd.

content_mine.fact: One artificial positive rating caused lasting positive herding in later ratings.
content_mine.beat: The visible attention leader becomes the expected winner.

content_mine.fact: Popularity information made success more unequal and less predictable in an experimental music market.
content_mine.beat: Early attention overwhelms differences in performance quality.

content_mine.fact: People concentrating on a demanding task can miss a highly visible unexpected event.
content_mine.beat: You alter the stage while every eye is fixed on the rival.

content_mine.fact: Applause spreads through local social influence as nearby people begin and stop clapping together.
content_mine.beat: One clap becomes the synchronized climax.

topics.twist: The remote controls attention through cameras too, so one televised use has made you capable of redirecting millions of people.
topics.ending: You learn that attention is neither talent nor love—it is an amplifier. Then someone watching remotely turns toward you before you press anything.

topics.title: What If You Controlled Every VIP List?
topics.premise: What if every 24 hours you could divide five VIP levels between yourself and one other person?
topics.world: Opening weekend at the Cannes Film Festival and Marché du Film, where badges, invitations and queue priority visibly decide who reaches buyers and premieres.

thumbnail.image: Your anxious face holds a glowing LEVEL 5 badge while your filmmaker sibling's scanner flashes LEVEL 0.

topics.rule: Choose one person every 24 hours. Their access plus yours must equal five: 5/0, 4/1 or 3/2. Every official scanner accepts the allocation, but access cannot make anyone inside listen or help.
topics.hook: Your badge reads Level 5, your sibling's reads 0, and the only buyer who might fund their film enters a premiere in 60 seconds.
beats: You transfer four levels; their scanner turns green while yours turns red.
Rewind to discovering that a 3/2 split admits both of you through restricted doors.
You must choose your dream producer's gala or your sibling's only buyer meeting.
You choose the sibling and are removed publicly from the carpet.
Consequence jump one: a rival takes your empty seat and turns your rejection into the festival's status joke.
At reset, you pair with the rival and select 5/0, locking them outside.
Consequence jump two: their cancelled meeting threatens projects and junior workers who had no role in the rivalry.
An executive offers to finance you if you remain Level 5 through the closing gala.
Your sibling simultaneously needs Level 4 to sign before their buyer leaves.
You choose 1/4, surrendering your meeting and public comeback.
Consequence jump three: an audit detects the impossible changes and deletes both identities from the festival.
Your humiliating removal footage is mistaken for a brilliant short film; buyers want it, and the badge relights with OSCAR ACCESS 0/5.
restarts: Level 5 still cannot guarantee that anyone listens.
Using 5/0 against the rival harms innocent workers.
The Level 1 humiliation becomes more valuable than VIP access.

topics.ending: You lose Cannes status but gain a project—and a new five-point allocation for a larger gatekeeping system.

topics.title: What If You Earned 1% of Everyone You Helped?
topics.premise: What if every time you helped someone succeed, 1% of all the money they made from that moment on flowed into your bank account forever?
topics.world: Present-day Shenzhen and Hong Kong, from the 10-story Huaqiangbei electronics stalls where hardware prototypes are born for $50 to Hong Kong's IFC venture-capital towers.

thumbnail.image: You handing a $5 screwdriver to a stressed street inventor while a glowing green '+1% FOREVER ($42,000/day)' tether connects him to your phone.

topics.rule: Whenever your direct help, introduction, or advice causes someone's income or company value to rise, an active '1.0% ROYALTY' link forms above them and deposits 1% of their net gain into your account every midnight. Limits: the help must be genuine and requested or accepted voluntarily. Catch: the 1% contract is symmetrical—if someone you backed causes financial ruin or fraud using the boost you gave them, 1% of their total damages is automatically deducted from your bank balance.
topics.hook: You lend a stranded courier in Shenzhen $10 for a replacement scooter battery, and at midnight your phone chimes with '+$4.80'—because you now own 1% of every delivery he makes for the rest of his life.
beats: Cold open: Outside Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei market, you lend a broke delivery rider ¥70 ($10) for a dead fuse; at midnight your HUD ticks 'ACTIVE ROYALTIES: 1 | +$4.80/DAY', and by Friday you're making $140 a month while sleeping. So what if you earned 1% of everyone you helped?

Baseline & rules: Helping 100 ordinary people with small favors earns you $500 a day; the rules become clear—only net new value counts, you can see each person's live '+$/hr' stream on your phone, and you cannot cancel a link once formed.

Jump 1 (The Huaqiangbei Talent Scout): Instead of chasing billionaires who don't need you, you walk the 30,000 tiny solder stalls of Huaqiangbei hunting for exhausted engineers one missing chip away from a breakthrough—buying a $400 oscilloscope for a twenty-year-old drone coder named Lin.

Complication: One of the stall owners you helped uses your introduction to sell counterfeit power banks that catch fire in a warehouse—and at midnight your phone flashes red: '-$18,200 (1% OF LIABILITY DAMAGES)'.

Jump 2 (The Power-Law Portfolio): You start vetting character as hard as talent; out of 40 micro-founders you help across Shenzhen and Hong Kong, 38 pay you $20 a day, one pays $4,000 a day, and Lin's agricultural drone startup lands a $90 million contract—paying you $900,000 overnight ('PORTFOLIO: +$34,000/DAY').

Early dilemma planted: Lin asks you to introduce him to Victor, a ruthless Hong Kong private-equity shark who can 10x the company before IPO; making the introduction will jump your 1% payout to $9,000,000, but you spot Victor cutting corners on flight-controller safety firmware.

Escalation: Blinded by the climb toward a $10M payout, you make the introduction anyway; Lin's valuation rockets to $800 million ahead of a dual Hong Kong–Nasdaq listing, and your live counter hits '+$112,000/DAY'.

The trap springs: The night before the IPO bell, Lin confesses to you in panic that Victor swapped the industrial solid-state relays in 50,000 cargo drones for cheap consumer chips to pad Q4 margins—and if they launch in monsoon season next month, crashes over urban highways will cause $4 billion in damages.

The math of ruin: One percent of a $4 billion catastrophe is '-$40,000,000'—enough to wipe out everything you own and put you $31 million in permanent debt, while blowing the whistle tonight kills the $8M IPO payout and tanks Lin's company to zero.

Climax choice: Ten minutes before the Hong Kong Exchange opening ceremony, you hand the hardware swap proof to the exchange regulator AND wire your entire $8.2 million accumulated royalty bankroll directly to Lin's factory to fund an emergency chip recall—watching your net balance drop to '$1,140' while saving Lin's company from Victor's fraud.

Callback & Part 2 twist: A month later, sitting at a Huaqiangbei noodle stall with $1,140 in your account, your phone chimes at midnight with '+$62,000'—because every one of the 1,200 factory workers whose jobs you saved just got linked to your 1% ledger at once.

Minute 6: Getting hit with a '-$18,200' liability deduction reveals you also own 1% of any disaster your people cause.
Minute 10: Discovering the $800M drone IPO hides a $4B hardware defect that will bankrupt both your friend and your 1% ledger unless you burn your own fortune to recall it.

topics.title: What If You Never Needed to Sleep Again?
topics.premise: What if your body stayed at 100% rested energy 24 hours a day, giving you 8 extra waking hours every single night while the rest of Earth was unconscious?
topics.world: Present-day Manhattan and the 24-hour global foreign-exchange desk linking Tokyo, London, and New York, where trillions of dollars move across three time zones that no single human can stay awake to trade.

thumbnail.image: You wide awake at glowing monitors at 3:00 AM with 'AWAKE: 1,400 HRS' floating beside your head, while exhausted bankers lie slumped across their desks around you.

topics.rule: Your body never builds adenosine or physical fatigue, keeping your reflexes and focus at a rested 9:00 AM baseline forever, tracked by a live 'HOURS AWAKE' and 'BRAIN STORAGE' HUD. Limits: you still age at normal calendar speed. Catch: sleep doesn't just rest muscles—it prunes 18% of daily brain synapses to clear useless noise. Without sleep, your brain never forgets a single background detail, steadily filling your finite neural working capacity toward 100.0%.
topics.hook: At 11:00 PM on a Tuesday, your roommate passes out exhausted, and for the first time in your life your energy bar locks at 100%—handing you a second full workday every single night while eight billion people lie unconscious.
beats: Cold open: At 3:14 AM in a silent New York diner, the cook is asleep on the counter while your HUD reads 'HOURS AWAKE: 72 | ENERGY: 100%', and you've already finished a week's worth of work since Monday. So what if you never needed to sleep again?

Baseline & rules: An average human sleeps 229,961 hours—26 full years of life—in the dark; you instantly gain 2,920 extra waking hours a year, an extra 15-month year inside every calendar year, with zero caffeine or grogginess.

Jump 1 (The 3-Session Edge): You take a night-desk seat at a midtown FX trading firm; while Tokyo traders sleep during New York hours and New York traders sleep during London open, you stay awake across all three shifts ('AWAKE: 480 HRS'), connecting order flows no single human trader has ever seen.

Complication: Around Hour 700, a second small readout appears under your awake counter: 'SYNAPTIC LOAD: 64.2%'—you realize you can still recite the license plate of every yellow cab that passed you three Tuesdays ago.

Jump 2 (The Human Bloomberg Terminal): Because your synapses never prune 18% at night, you become a walking cross-market pattern engine, spotting a hidden 0.4-second arbitrage lag between Zurich Swiss Franc futures and Singapore gold desks to clear $8.4 million in thirty days.

Early dilemma planted: Your younger sister Maya visits New York for a weekend; while talking to her, your brain involuntarily overlays 4,000 stray prices, footsteps, and ceiling-fan rotations ('SYNAPTIC LOAD: 82.9%'), and she asks why you look through her like a screen.
Escalation: Rival funds hire three-person relay teams to beat you, but handoff notes lose 40% of context; your uninterrupted 1,800-hour streak lets you corner a $600 million sovereign bond spread.

The trap springs: At Hour 2,100, your HUD flashes red: 'SYNAPTIC SATURATION: 98.7% — OVERFLOW IN 4 HOURS'; without night-time glymphatic pruning, your visual cortex starts replaying Tuesday's order books on top of live Manhattan traffic.

The discovery: A neurologist friend runs an fMRI on you and is stunned—your brain has zero physical damage, buffer-overflowing only because every millisecond of the last 90 days is locked at equal priority; the only way to free 30% capacity without sleeping is transcranial magnetic erasure of one dense emotional memory cluster.

Climax choice: With the Bank of Japan rate decision 12 minutes away (worth $45 million on your open position) and your HUD at '99.8%', you can either wipe the dense high-resolution memory cluster of your childhood summers with Maya to keep the trade data, or dump the entire 90-day trading ledger from your cortex to save your memories of her.

Callback & Part 2 twist: Sitting in the same 3:14 AM diner with Maya after wiping the $45M trade ledger ('SYNAPTIC LOAD: 71.0%'), you look out the window at the empty street—and spot a woman across the avenue staring straight at you with a HUD over HER head reading 'HOURS AWAKE: 41,000'.
restarts: Minute 3: Turning 8 spare hours a night into a monopoly across the Tokyo-London-New York currency handoff.
Minute 7: Discovering 'Synaptic Load'—without nightly pruning, your brain cannot delete background noise.
Minute 11: Hitting 99.8% neural saturation minutes before a $45M central-bank trade, forcing you to choose which memories to erase.

content_mine.fact: In 1964, 17-year-old Randy Gardner set the scientifically monitored human wakefulness record at 264.4 hours (11 days and 25 minutes), after which Guinness World Records permanently retired the category due to lethal health risks.
content_mine.beat: Cold open & baseline: passing the 264-hour human limit at 100% energy.

content_mine.fact: Sleeping 8 hours a night consumes 2,920 hours every year—meaning an 80-year-old has spent 26.6 years (233,600 hours) completely unconscious.
content_mine.beat: Baseline: calculating the 26 extra years of waking life you unlock.

content_mine.fact: The global foreign exchange (FX) market trades $7.5 trillion per day continuously 24 hours a day across four major handoffs—Sydney, Tokyo, London, and New York—with the London-New York overlap alone handling over 50% of volume.
content_mine.beat: Jump 1: becoming the only human trader awake across all three global sessions without a relay handoff.

content_mine.fact: Neuroscientists Giulio Tononi and Chiara Cirelli's 'Synaptic Homeostasis Hypothesis' (SHY) showed via 3D electron microscopy that sleep shrinks brain synapses by 18% each night to prune irrelevant daily data and restore learning capacity.
content_mine.beat: Complication: why skipping sleep means your synapses never prune 18% of daily background noise.

content_mine.fact: In 2013, Dr. Maiken Nedergaard discovered the brain's 'glymphatic system', proving that during deep sleep, brain interstitial space expands by 60% so cerebrospinal fluid can flush metabolic waste at 10x the waking rate.
content_mine.beat: Complication: explaining why normal humans die without sleep while your modified biology bypasses fatigue but keeps every synapse.

content_mine.fact: Patient 'AJ' (Jill Price), the first documented case of Hyperthymestic Syndrome (Highly Superior Autobiographical Memory) studied at UC Irvine, described her inability to forget every calendar day since age 14 as 'a running movie that never stops and exhausts me'.
content_mine.beat: Early dilemma: why remembering every cab license plate and ceiling fan rotation at Hour 1,200 crowds out real conversation with Maya.

content_mine.fact: Medical and financial shift-handoff studies (New England Journal of Medicine) show that up to 30% to 40% of critical contextual information is lost or distorted whenever a day shift hands off a complex position to a night shift.
content_mine.beat: Escalation: why three-person rival trading relays still lose to your single continuous consciousness.

content_mine.fact: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) breakdown during waking hours steadily fills A1 receptors in the basal forebrain to create 'sleep pressure', which caffeine only masks temporarily by blocking the receptor without clearing the chemical.
content_mine.beat: Baseline: why your co-workers crash after four espressos at 3:00 AM while your adenosine stays at zero.

content_mine.fact: Paul Reber at Northwestern University calculated the human brain's functional storage across 86 billion neurons and 100 trillion synapses at roughly 2.5 petabytes—equivalent to 3 million hours of continuous HD video.
content_mine.beat: The trap springs: why unpruned hyper-resolution sensory recording drives your active working cortex to 98.7% saturation.

content_mine.fact: A rare mutation in the DEC2 (BHLHE41) gene identified by UCSF geneticist Ying-Hui Fu allows 'natural short sleepers' (less than 1% of humanity) to thrive on 4 hours of sleep with zero cognitive deficit.
content_mine.beat: The discovery: the neurologist comparing your scan to DEC2 short-sleepers.

content_mine.fact: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) targeted at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex can selectively disrupt reconsolidation of specific reactivated memory traces in human clinical trials.
content_mine.beat: Climax choice: using targeted TMS reconsolidation disruption to choose between wiping the $45M trade book or your childhood memories.

content_mine.fact: The Bank of Japan's July 2024 monetary policy shift triggered a $6.4 trillion global 'yen carry trade' unwind in 72 hours, swinging USD/JPY by over 12% and wiping out leveraged funds in minutes.
content_mine.beat: Climax choice: the 12-minute countdown to the Bank of Japan rate decision.

topics.twist: Your brain wasn't running out of energy—it was running out of forgetting, and when you step back into the 3:00 AM city, you discover a tiny underground class of 'Sleepless' who have been awake for years.
topics.ending: You'll never resent going to bed the same way once you realize sleep isn't the tax on your day—it's the delete key that keeps you sane.

topics.title: What If Your Vote Counted as 51% Every Time?
topics.premise: What if your single vote counted as 51 percent of every vote you ever took part in?
topics.world: Glarus, Switzerland, in francs, today: a canton that still votes by raising hands in the town square, in a country that votes on nearly everything, including cow horns.

thumbnail.image: A packed town square with every hand raised one way; you alone, sleepy, raising one finger the other way; a giant in-world scoreboard above reads 51% on your side; the mayor clutching his head.

topics.rule: In any real vote you are entitled to join, your ballot weighs 51 percent of the total. Catch: it only beats a simple majority (two-thirds and unanimous rules still stand), the published result always shows your 51, and you cannot abstain: if you are in the room, your true preference is counted.
topics.hook: Six thousand people in a Swiss square raise their hands for 'yes'. You, at the back, half asleep, scratch your ear. The teller counts, turns white, and announces: 'no' wins, 51 to 49.
beats: Cold open: the ear scratch (absurd detail), the square, the scoreboard stamping 51%.
Rules; the baseline against you: the chance that one ordinary vote decides a big election is around one in tens of millions. Yours is one in one.
The fun, small: pizza toppings, the class trip, the film on movie night, the village talent show (you make your friend Jonas's yodelling goat act win). 51% every time.
Jump 1: your school, your football club and the fire brigade all realise that any vote with you in it is over. Half the town courts you; the other half stops inviting you.
The promised dilemma: the mayor, Frau Elmer, says it kindly: 'If you always win, why would the rest of us ever raise a hand again?'
Jump 2, money and power: one share in a company gets you into a shareholder vote. One share, 51%. A boardroom of grey suits watches a teenager with a cheese sandwich replace the chairman.
Catch 1: you cannot abstain. A vote you wanted to stay out of (Jonas against his own sister for club captain) reads your heart and counts it. Jonas sees the 51.

Catch 2: the town fights back with maths. A new bylaw: everything needs two-thirds. Your 51 is now short by about 16 points, so you need a third of the others to agree with you. For the first time you have to persuade somebody.
Jump 3, the big scale: the national referendum Sunday. You are one Swiss voter among five million, and your ballot is 51% of the country. Bern has noticed the pattern in Glarus.

Climax choice: the square votes on a motion to switch the two-thirds rule back to simple majority. Procedural votes need only a simple majority, so you can hand yourself the town forever with one raised hand, or keep your hand down in front of everyone and stay beatable. Abstaining is impossible: your real wish will be counted. What do you actually want?
Callback and twist: the teller counts, turns white again. The result is 51 to 49, against what you wanted. Somebody else in the square is scratching their ear.
restarts: About 3 min: from pizza to power (the one-share boardroom).
About 6 min: you can't abstain; the power reads your heart.
About 9 min: two-thirds, the town out-thinks you.
End: a second 51 percent.

topics.title: What If You Were Forgotten Every Midnight?
topics.premise: What if every person on Earth forgot you existed at midnight, every night, while every record of you stayed?
topics.world: A Mediterranean island town of 2,000 with one ferry, in euros, today: forgetting is strangest where everybody knows everybody and has known you since birth.

thumbnail.image: You in your own doorway holding a birthday cake; your family at the table staring at you like a burglar; over your head a glowing label: KNOWN BY: 0.

topics.rule: At 00:00 every human loses every memory of you. Paper, photos, bank records and your dog are untouched. People can re-learn you in a day, then lose it again. Catch: debts, crimes and promises on paper stay yours, and nobody remembers why they owe you anything.
topics.hook: It is your birthday. You walk into your own kitchen with the cake and your mother picks up a frying pan. The photo of you two is on the wall right behind her.
beats: Cold open: the frying pan, the photo on the wall, the dog (absurd detail) greeting you like a king while the family calls the police.

Rules; the readout KNOWN BY: 0 climbs through the day as you introduce yourself and snaps back at midnight. Baseline: a first impression forms in about 100 milliseconds, and you now get a new one from everyone daily.
The scheming phase: you A/B-test your own personality. Same job interview five days running; day 5 you are hired in four minutes. Laugh and triumph.
Jump 1: zero reputation means zero embarrassment. You sing at the festival, ask out the ferry captain's daughter Lia 12 different ways, and keep the version that works.
Catch 1: records stay. The bank has your loan on file, the teller has never seen you; the town now has a 'ghost resident' with a house, a tax bill and no face.
Jump 2: you get rich in favours the slow way. A notebook the whole town signs each day, 'I, the baker, owe this stranger one loaf'; paper remembers what people cannot.
The promised dilemma: Lia writes herself a letter each night about you. Each morning she reads it and has to decide to believe her own handwriting.
Strange discovery: the baker bags your usual order before you speak and cannot say why. Hands and feelings keep something that memory drops.
Jump 3, the big scale: the mainland notices the island's impossible paperwork; a reporter arrives and you could become the most famous person no one remembers.

Climax choice: an offer to leave on the ferry as a legend on paper everywhere, or stay and spend every day earning the same 2,000 people from zero. Leaving costs Lia's daily letter; staying costs the world.

Callback and twist: midnight on your next birthday. You brace in the kitchen doorway with the cake. The readout ticks to KNOWN BY: 1. Not your mother. Someone outside the window is writing your name down.

topics.title: What If You Saw How Much People Respect You?
topics.premise: What if a glowing score from 0 to 100 floated over every person's head showing how much they actually respect you in real time?
topics.world: Present-day Tokyo, from a neon izakaya in Shimbashi to a 40th-floor zaibatsu boardroom in Marunouchi, where polite bows hide ruthless hierarchy ('tatemae' vs 'honne').

thumbnail.image: Your smiling coworker bowing deeply to you with 'RESPECT: 4/100' glowing red above his head, while a stone-faced executive in the elevator behind him has a glowing gold '94/100'.

topics.rule: A floating integer from 0 to 100 above every person's head shows their true, unconscious respect for you right now, updating the millisecond you speak or act. Limits: it only shows the score from 0 to 100, never why it moved. Catch: the human brain cannot distinguish genuine admiration from intimidation on the meter—and anyone whose score hits 100/100 becomes psychologically unable to question or warn you when you are wrong.
topics.hook: Your junior teammate bows at forty-five degrees and calls you 'Senpai'—while the glowing red number over his head drops from 6 out of 100 to 3.
beats: Cold open: At a Friday night izakaya in Shimbashi, your loudest workplace flatterer toasts your health with a glowing '4/100' over his head, while the quiet night-shift security guard who never speaks to you has '81/100'. So what if you saw how much people respect you?

Baseline & rules: On the Yamanote Line train, strangers start at a neutral '50/100'; slouching and apologizing for nothing drops the whole carriage to '34/100', while calmly holding the door for an elderly commuter bumps seven strangers to '68/100'.

Jump 1 (Office reversal): In the Marunouchi tower, you stop laughing at your manager's bad jokes ('19/100') and calmly reject an unpaid weekend dump; his face turns purple, yet his number jumps from '19' to '64' in two seconds.
Complication: Your best friend Kenji sits at a warm '84/100', but whenever you use your new cold status tricks to impress executives around him, Kenji's score quietly ticks down: '84... 76... 69'.

Jump 2 (High-stakes negotiation): You're sent as a sacrificial junior to a hostile supplier negotiation in Osaka; by watching which sentences make the rival CEO's meter tick up ('41 -> 58 -> 79'), you map his hidden values in real time and close a ¥4 billion contract without offering a discount.

Early dilemma planted: You notice that making a junior analyst terrified of firing raises his score to '91/100' just as fast as mentoring him—because the meter measures deference, whether born of awe or fear.

Escalation: Addicted to high scores, you optimize every pause, suit, and silence until everyone on the 40th floor walks past you at '95/100' or higher, and you're promoted to lead the company's flagship lithium-battery acquisition.

The trap springs: During final due diligence, your whole team of '99/100' analysts nods in unison at your valuation model—while Kenji, now down at '52/100', tries to hand you a red-flagged lab report that you wave away because 'a 52 doesn't know better than five 99s'.

The crisis: Ten minutes before the live Tokyo Stock Exchange signing, you finally glance at the lab report and realize the target factory's thermal runaway test was falsified—and your '99/100' team stayed silent because your aura hit '100/100' and froze their willingness to contradict you.

Climax choice: On stage under the cameras with the board watching at '98/100', the only way to void the ¥40 billion contract legally is to publicly admit an embarrassing calculation blunder of your own—watching thirty executives' meters plummet from '98' to '7/100' in one breath while Kenji's lone number in the back row climbs back to '96/100'.

Callback & Part 2 twist: Back at the Shimbashi izakaya with Kenji at '96/100', you catch your reflection in the glass behind the bar—and realize there is a number floating above YOUR own head, currently reading '38/100'.
restarts: Minute 3: Discovering that saying 'no' raises respect faster than doing favors flips how you play the office.
Minute 7: Realizing the meter merges fear and admiration into the same number turns your climb into a psychological trap.
Minute 11: Hitting '100/100' with your team silences the only people who know your ¥40B deal is a disaster.

topics.title: What If You Saw How Badly People Want Things?
topics.premise: What if a glowing percentage bar from 0% to 100% floated over everyone's head showing how badly they want whatever they are looking at right now?
topics.world: Present-day Macau and Hong Kong, moving from high-stakes VIP baccarat and poker rooms on the Cotai Strip to Sotheby's evening auctions and private waterfront real-estate negotiations.

thumbnail.image: A stone-faced billionaire in a suit saying 'Not interested' at an auction table while a blazing violet 'WANT: 99.9%' bar erupts above his head as you hold the paddle.

topics.rule: Whenever someone looks at an object, contract, card, or person, a live percentage from 0.0% to 100.0% floats over their head showing how badly they want it right now, plus their secret walk-away price. Limits: they must be looking directly at or thinking about a specific target within 30 feet. Catch: when a human's desire meter hits 100.0%, the bar turns violet—meaning their rational walk-away limit is gone and there is no law or boundary they won't cross to take it from you.
topics.hook: A luxury watch dealer in Hong Kong sighs and says your grandfather's scratched steel chronograph is barely worth $400—while the glowing bar above his head screams 'WANT: 98.6% | MAX PRICE: $85,000'.
beats: Cold open: In a Tsim Sha Tsui watch shop, a bored dealer offers you $400 for an old steel watch while his HUD flashes 'WANT: 98.6% | WALK-AWAY: $85,000'; you smile, say '$84,500 or I walk', and he wires the cash in ninety seconds. So what if you saw how badly people want things?

Baseline & rules: Every negotiation on Earth is a game of hiding how badly you want the deal; at '0–30%' the bar is cool blue, at '70–99%' it burns orange-red, and it updates the instant someone glances at a target.

Jump 1 (The Macau Poker & Antique Run): You take the ferry to Macau's Cotai Strip; at the No-Limit Hold'em tables, whenever an opponent stares at the pot with 'WANT: 94%' on a river bet, you know he wants you to fold (bluff), whereas 'WANT: 99%' looking at your chip stack means he holds the nuts—turning $800 into $320,000 in one weekend.

Complication: In your personal life, seeing desire bars is hilarious and brutal—your friend claims he's 'on a strict diet' while staring at your fries at '97.4%', and a date who acts aloof hits '91%' whenever you mention leaving early.

Jump 2 (High-End Real Estate & Art Brokerage): You set up as a bespoke buyer's agent in Hong Kong's Peak district; by watching sellers' bars when you threaten to walk ('WANT TO SELL TODAY: 96.2%'), you shave $4.2 million off a harbourfront villa and pocket a $420,000 fee.

Early dilemma planted: Your younger brother Theo is desperate to buy back the small harbor ferry repair yard your late father lost to a creditor; Theo's bar is at '99.1%', and the creditor knows it, demanding $3 million for a yard worth $900,000.

Escalation: To raise the $3M in one night, you enter a private Sotheby's Hong Kong evening auction to run 'reverse arbitrage'—spotting which billionaire bidders are at '99.5%' and forcing them to buy you out of competing bids.

The trap springs: On Lot 44—an unassuming 18th-century porcelain vase estimated at $200,000—two rival tycoons in the front row both cross '99.9%' and their bars turn solid violet: '100.0% — NO LIMIT'; you raise the paddle to $4.8 million expecting them to pay you to step aside, and the auctioneer unexpectedly drops the hammer on YOU when one tycoon suffers a coughing fit.

The crisis: In the VIP settlement lounge, the losing tycoon's head of security locks the door—his boss's bar is still violet '100.0%', not because of the porcelain, but because a microfilm ledger of offshore bribes from 1996 is sealed inside the vase's false ceramic base, and he will pay zero dollars if he takes it off your body in the parking garage.

Climax choice: With the tycoon and his rival both entering the VIP room at violet '100.0%', you hold the vase over the marble balcony railing ('DROP THREAT: 99%')—forcing the two rival tycoons to bid against each other in real-time wire transfers straight to your brother's dockyard escrow ($3.2M... $5.0M... $7.5M) before smashing the empty porcelain shell on the floor and handing the microfilm to both of them so neither has leverage over the other.

Callback & Part 2 twist: The next morning at your brother's reclaimed ferry yard, Theo hugs you with his bar finally resting at a calm blue '12% (CONTENT)'—until a quiet harbor customs inspector walks past the drydock, glances at the rusted hull of an old tugboat inside, and his bar spikes straight to violet '100.0%'.
restarts: Minute 3: Moving from street haggling to reading river bluffs and nut hands in Macau VIP poker rooms.
Minute 7: Using seller desperation meters to shave millions off Hong Kong Peak real estate to fund your brother's dockyard.
Minute 10: Triggering a violet '100.0% NO LIMIT' obsession at a Sotheby's auction over a vase hiding a blackmail ledger.

content_mine.fact: Harvard Negotiation Project co-founder Howard Raiffa proved that in any two-party negotiation, the 'Zone of Possible Agreement' (ZOPA) is bounded by each side's secret 'Reservation Price' (walk-away number)—and the party who knows the other's reservation price captures 85% to 95% of the entire surplus.
content_mine.beat: Cold open & Baseline: why seeing the watch dealer's $85,000 reservation price lets you capture $84,500 on the spot.

content_mine.fact: A 1968 Rolex Cosmograph Daytona 'Paul Newman' reference 6239 originally retailed for $210 in steel, yet unpolished examples discovered in drawers routinely sell for $80,000 to $300,000 (with Newman's own reaching $17.8 million at Phillips).
content_mine.beat: Cold open: why the Tsim Sha Tsui dealer offers $400 for a steel chronograph worth $85,000.

content_mine.fact: University of Chicago biopsychologist Eckhard Hess proved in 1960 ('Pupillometrics') that human pupils involuntarily dilate by 18% to 25% within 300 milliseconds of seeing an object they strongly desire—which is why 17th-century Chinese jade merchants wore dark smoky-quartz spectacles during bidding.
content_mine.beat: Baseline & Jump 1: the real biological basis of hidden desire cues in Chinese merchants and Macau card players.

content_mine.fact: Macau's gaming revenue reached $22.7 billion in 2023—more than double the Las Vegas Strip—where high-stakes No-Limit Hold'em games in Cotai regularly feature single pots exceeding $500,000.
content_mine.beat: Jump 1: turning $800 into $320,000 by reading desire bars on river bets in Macau.

content_mine.fact: Nobel laureate Richard Thaler documented the 'Winner's Curse' in auctions: when competitive desire ('auction fever') takes over, bidders systematically overpay by 30% to 50% above an asset's rational value just to beat a rival.
content_mine.beat: Escalation & The trap springs: two rival tycoons pushing a $200,000 porcelain lot to $4.8M as their bars hit 100.0%.

content_mine.fact: At Christie's 2017 auction of 'Salvator Mundi', two Gulf bidders—neither knowing they were both bidding as proxies for allies—drove a $100 million pre-sale estimate to a world-record $450.3 million in 19 minutes of ego escalation.
content_mine.beat: The trap springs: real auction history of two tycoons hitting 100% status obsession on a single lot.

content_mine.fact: Under New York and international auction law, auctioneers are legally permitted to take 'chandelier bids' (imaginary bids off the wall or chandelier) up to the seller's secret reserve price to create the illusion of competing demand.
content_mine.beat: Escalation: spotting when the auctioneer's own desire bar shows he's bluffing off the chandelier vs real bidders.

content_mine.fact: Hong Kong's Victoria Peak ('The Peak') holds the world record for residential land prices per square foot, where single houses on Pollock's Path and Mount Nicholson sell for $150 million to $350 million USD.
content_mine.beat: Jump 2: shaving $4.2M off a Peak villa by catching the seller's '96.2% NEED LIQUIDITY TODAY' bar.

content_mine.fact: In 2010, a 1740 Qianlong-era Chinese porcelain vase found in a suburban London house clearance with a £1,200 estimate triggered a ferocious bidding war among Chinese collectors and hammered for £43 million ($69.3 million).
content_mine.beat: The trap springs: why an 18th-century porcelain vase at Sotheby's Hong Kong draws ruthless billionaire bidding.

content_mine.fact: Game theorist Thomas Schelling (2005 Nobel Prize) proved in 'The Strategy of Conflict' that the only way a weaker party can defeat a stronger opponent at 100% aggression is a credible 'Brinkmanship Threat' to destroy the prize both sides want.
content_mine.beat: Climax choice: holding the vase over the marble balcony railing so both tycoons wire $7.5M to your brother's escrow.

content_mine.fact: Caltech neuroeconomist Antonio Rangel showed via fMRI that the medial orbitofrontal cortex computes a real-time numerical 'Willingness-to-Pay' (WTP) signal for every object a human looks at, even when they consciously deny wanting it.
content_mine.beat: Baseline & Complication: how the human brain calculates an exact secret Willingness-to-Pay number in milliseconds.

content_mine.fact: Neuroscientist Wolfram Schultz proved that dopamine neurons do not fire for pleasure upon owning something—they fire for 'Wanting' (anticipation error) and drop back to baseline the moment the object is secured.
content_mine.beat: Callback: why Theo's bar drops from '99.1%' to a peaceful '12%' once the dockyard is safe.

topics.twist: A 99% bar makes you rich because people will overpay—but a violet 100.0% bar means they will stop bidding with money and take it by force, forcing you to use Nobel game-theory brinkmanship to survive.
topics.ending: You'll never negotiate a salary, a car, or a relationship the same way once you realize the person who wants it less always owns the room.

topics.title: What If Everything Had a Durability Bar?
topics.premise: What if every machine, bridge, contract, and alibi had a glowing video-game durability bar counting down to the exact second it breaks?
topics.world: Present-day Rotterdam and the North Sea, the world's busiest heavy-industry port where 400-meter container ships, offshore oil rigs, and $100M salvage contracts operate at the edge of metal fatigue.

thumbnail.image: You on an airport tarmac pointing at a gleaming jet engine with a flashing red 'DURABILITY: 0.2%' bar above it, while passengers board happily behind you.

topics.rule: Everything you look at displays a percentage bar from 100.0% to 0.0% showing how close it is to structural failure, plus the exact stress cycle that will snap it. Limits: you must have direct line-of-sight within 50 meters, and you cannot see inside sealed buildings from outside. Catch: repairing or stopping one failure at 0.1% redirects the physical or financial load onto the next weakest link in the system—and the bar also appears over human agreements and trust.
topics.hook: You're boarding a brand-new budget flight in Rotterdam when you glance out the oval window at the left wing pylon—and see a flashing red bar reading 'DURABILITY: 0.1% — WILL SNAP ON LANDING'.
beats: Cold open: On the tarmac at Rotterdam Airport, a rusty $4 baggage cart reads 'DURABILITY: 94.2%', while the gleaming turbine pylon on Flight 402 flashes '0.1%'; you fake a panic attack at the boarding door to force a safety inspection, and mechanics pull a cracked titanium bolt from the wing ten minutes later. So what if everything had a durability bar?

Baseline & rules: You test the bar in your kitchen—your 'replace every 3 months' water filter sits at '88%', a cheap 1990s toaster sits at '99.1%', and your brand-new smartphone battery is secretly at '31%'.

Jump 1 (Scrapyard & Car Flipping): At the Rotterdam harbor vehicle auctions, you buy 'high-mileage' diesel vans whose engines read '96% DURABILITY' for €2,000 while skipping shiny low-mileage luxury cars sitting at '4.2% (Timing Chain Imminent)', clearing €180,000 in six weeks.
Complication: You notice the bar doesn't just measure steel—when two port contractors shake hands on a delivery deadline, a bar appears between them reading 'CONTRACT DURABILITY: 12%'.

Jump 2 (Maritime Salvage & Shorting): You partner with an independent tugboat captain, Bram, using Lloyd's Open Form 'No Cure, No Pay' salvage rules; by positioning your tug 5 miles off ships whose rudders read '0.8%', you legally claim 15% salvage awards worth €6.5 million when they lose steering in the English Channel.
Early dilemma planted: Above your partnership with Bram floats 'TRUST DURABILITY: 92%'—every time you refuse to explain HOW you know which ship will snap next, it ticks down: '92%... 78%... 61%'.
Escalation: A major North Sea energy conglomerate hires you for €50,000 a day to walk their offshore platforms and point out hidden subsea riser cracks before they blow.

The trap springs: On the Goliath Alpha platform during a Force 9 gale, you tell the chief engineer to shut down Riser Pipe B ('0.3%')—and the instant the valve closes, the pressure reroutes into the main sea-floor blowout preventer, dropping its bar from '48.0%' to '1.4%' in ten seconds.

The crisis: Evacuating the rig will cost the conglomerate €200 million and get Bram's salvage license revoked for 'false alarm sabotage' unless the pipe actually ruptures—and your 'TRUST DURABILITY' with Bram sits at '4.0%'.

Climax choice: With the blowout preventer ticking down ('0.9%... 0.6%'), you manually pull the emergency subsea shear-ram lever yourself—saving all 84 crew and preventing a North Sea spill, even though the shear-ram destroys €90M of intact drill pipe and drops your 'CAREER & TRUST DURABILITY' with Bram to '0.0%' as he turns you in to maritime police.

Callback & Part 2 twist: Six months later, Bram visits you at the Rotterdam dock after an acoustic X-ray finally proves the blowout preventer was 3 millimeters from exploding ('TRUST DURABILITY: RESTORED TO 100%')—and as you look up at the port's massive Maeslantkering storm-surge barrier holding back the North Sea, its bar flickers to '0.4%'.
restarts: Minute 3: Moving from consumer planned-obsolescence hacks to €6.5M 'No Cure, No Pay' maritime salvage in the English Channel.
Minute 7: Discovering the load-transfer catch—saving one failing part at 0.3% slams the pressure into the next pipe down the line.
Minute 11: Triggering the subsea shear-ram on the North Sea rig before it breaks, sacrificing your own career bar to save 84 lives.

content_mine.fact: American Airlines Flight 191 crashed in 1979 after a 10-inch fatigue crack in the left engine pylon bulkhead—caused by an improper forklift maintenance shortcut—snapped during takeoff rotation.
content_mine.beat: Cold open: spotting the '0.1%' durability bar on the jet engine pylon bolt.

content_mine.fact: In 1924, the secret 'Phoebus Cartel' formed by Osram, Philips, and General Electric fined manufacturers if their light bulbs lasted longer than 1,000 hours—even though the Livermore Centennial Bulb has burned continuously for over 1,000,000 hours since 1901.
content_mine.beat: Baseline: why modern appliances show '31%' durability out of the box while an old toaster sits at '99.1%'.

content_mine.fact: Reliability engineers model mechanical lifespans using the 'Bathtub Curve' (Weibull distribution): high 'infant mortality' failures in brand-new parts, a long flat mid-life, and a steep wear-out cliff.
content_mine.beat: Jump 1: why brand-new luxury engines with manufacturing defects sit at '4.2%' while broken-in diesel vans sit at '96%'.

content_mine.fact: Under the centuries-old 'Lloyd's Open Form' (LOF) maritime salvage law and the 1989 International Salvage Convention, a tugboat that rescues a disabled vessel in danger is legally awarded 10% to 50% of the saved ship and cargo's total value.
content_mine.beat: Jump 2: earning €6.5 million with Bram by parking a tugboat near ships at '0.8%' rudder durability.

content_mine.fact: The Port of Rotterdam is Europe's largest seaport, stretching 42 kilometers and handling 438 million tonnes of cargo and 30,000 ocean-going ships per year.
content_mine.beat: World & Jump 1: why Rotterdam's 30,000 ships per year make it the ultimate hunting ground for durability bars.

content_mine.fact: Aloha Airlines Flight 243 lost an 18-foot section of its upper fuselage at 24,000 feet in 1988 after 89,680 short-hop pressurization cycles caused 'multiple-site fatigue cracking' invisible to routine visual checks.
content_mine.beat: Escalation: explaining how micro-cracks accumulate across thousands of pressure cycles while looking normal on the surface.

content_mine.fact: In cascading grid and pipeline failures (studied by ETH Zurich's Dirk Helbing), shutting down one overloaded node redistributes 100% of its flow to adjacent nodes, accelerating secondary failure by up to 400%.
content_mine.beat: The trap springs: why closing Riser Pipe B at '0.3%' slams the blowout preventer from '48%' down to '1.4%'.

content_mine.fact: The 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster was triggered when high-pressure methane gas bypassed a failed cement seal and a bent drill pipe prevented the blowout preventer's blind shear rams from sealing the well, costing BP $65 billion.
content_mine.beat: Climax choice: why firing the blind shear rams at '0.6%' before the pipe bends is the only way to save the rig.

content_mine.fact: Ultrasonic phased-array and radiographic X-ray non-destructive testing (NDT) can detect internal hydrogen-induced sub-surface cracks as small as 0.5 millimeters inside 50-millimeter steel walls.
content_mine.beat: Callback: how the post-incident ultrasonic X-ray vindicates you and restores Bram's trust bar to '100%'.

content_mine.fact: The collapse of Genoa's Morandi Bridge in 2018 occurred because salt-air corrosion ate through steel stay cables hidden inside poured concrete sleeves where visual inspectors could not see them.
content_mine.beat: Escalation: spotting hidden internal corrosion inside concrete and steel jackets.

content_mine.fact: Organizational psychologist Kurt Dirks' empirical studies on interpersonal trust show that trust exhibits dramatic 'asymmetry': a single unexplained action can erode 50% to 80% of accumulated trust, requiring 5x to 10x as many consistent proofs to rebuild.
content_mine.beat: Early dilemma: watching Bram's 'TRUST DURABILITY' bar drop every time you keep your power secret.

content_mine.fact: Rotterdam's Maeslantkering storm-surge barrier consists of two hollow floating steel arms—each as long as the Eiffel Tower is tall (210 meters) and pivoted on a single 680-ton spherical ball joint—protecting 1.5 million people below sea level.
content_mine.beat: Part 2 twist: looking up at the Maeslantkering ball joint as its bar flickers to '0.4%'.

topics.twist: Preventing a disaster when the bar is at 0.6% looks identical to sabotage to everyone who can't see the bar—until the X-ray comes back six months later, right as the storm barrier holding back the North Sea drops to 0.4%.
topics.ending: You'll never cross a bridge or make a promise the same way once you realize nothing breaks all at once—everything counts down by 0.1% while nobody is looking.

topics.title: What If You Were the 2nd Best at Everything?
topics.premise: What if you were instantly the second-best person alive at anything you tried, and could never, ever be first?
topics.world: Kingston, Jamaica, at the school sprint championships ('Champs'), then outward: the one place where finishing second in a 100 m is a national event.

thumbnail.image: You on a podium's second step, bored, wearing a dozen silver medals; beside you the stunned world champion on the top step looking down at you in fear; a glowing #2 over your head.

topics.rule: The moment you seriously try something, you perform as the second-best living human at it. You beat everyone but the current number one, to whom you always lose. Catch: if number one quits, someone else becomes number one; you can never win anything that only has one prize.
topics.hook: You have never run a race in your life. The gun goes, and you cross the line 0.11 seconds behind the fastest schoolboy in Jamaica, in borrowed shoes, eating a patty.
beats: Cold open: the patty, the photo finish, the crowd silent; the readout over your head stamps #2.
Rules; the baseline against you: the fastest man ever ran 9.58, the second fastest 9.69, and you can name only one of them.
Testing spree, the fun: chess café (you lose only to one teenager online), a piano, a patois rap battle, parallel parking. A counter starts: #2 IN: 14 THINGS.
Jump 1, money: second place pays. Prize money, sponsors who love 'the kid who is silver in everything'; #2 IN: 300 THINGS.
The promised dilemma: your cousin Dre is the real island number one in the 100 m, and the national selectors only take one.
Catch 1: winner-take-all fields. One job, one scholarship, one girl's prom yes, and you are the best loser alive; a montage of gracious runner-up speeches gets a laugh and then stings.
Jump 2, scheming: you hunt fields where being second is everything. Second opinion doctor's assistant, co-pilot, vice-captain, understudy: the world runs on number twos.

Jump 3, the big scale: every number one on Earth starts hearing about you. They cannot be beaten by you, but they can be exhausted by you; the chess champion plays you 40 games straight and wins by less each time.
Strange test: you try something only one person does, being your mother's favourite. The readout says #2. You are an only child.

Climax choice: Dre pulls a hamstring before the final. If he withdraws you are still second, behind a stranger; if you coach him through it with second-best-in-the-world coaching, he wins and you are publicly the one who lost. You choose the loss that costs your one shot at selection.
Callback and twist: same finish line, same patty. The readout flickers on one line only: #1. At something you never tried. And a second kid in the crowd has #2 over her head, looking straight at you.

topics.premise: What if your body could store 100 kilojoules whenever you slowed down and release it through one explosive sprint?

topics.rule: You capture mechanical energy from your own deceleration instead of losing it as heat. Capacity is 100 kJ, leakage is 5% per minute, and release must pass through your own muscles or pedals.

topics.premise: What if you knew everything there is to know for one minute a day, and kept only what you managed to write down?
topics.world: A court-reporting school in Chicago, today, in dollars: you are a trainee stenographer, the fastest way a human can get words out, which is the only thing that matters when all knowledge lasts 60 seconds.

thumbnail.image: You at a desk, eyes blazing white, hand a blur over a page; a glowing in-world clock reads 0:07; behind you a professor drops his coffee at what is on the page.

topics.rule: Once a day you say 'start' and for exactly 60 seconds you know everything that is true right now (not the future). Catch: the you inside the minute knows more than you do and decides what to write, so you wake up holding orders with no reasons.
topics.hook: You wake up with a pen in your fist and your own handwriting up your arm: DON'T TRUST THE LANDLORD. BUY EGGS. You wrote it a minute ago, when you knew everything, and now you have no idea why.
beats: Cold open: the arm note, the eggs, a clock on the wall frozen at 0:00; you obey the egg part and feel stupid.
Rules in three lines; the baseline against you: speech carries about 39 bits a second, so the whole universe has to fit through a straw 60 seconds long.
Day 2 you waste it: you spend 40 seconds just staring, awed, and write one word, 'WOW'. Laugh.
You train like an athlete: steno machine, 225 words a minute, a prepared question list; first clean win, tomorrow's exam answers, and the teacher squints.
Jump 1, money and status: the minute-you writes one line that fixes a bug a company posted a bounty on; your name gets around school; the landlord suddenly gets friendly.
The promised dilemma surfaces: one note ends 'do NOT ask about Maya'. Maya is your best friend. You now can't stop wondering what you know for a minute a day.
Jump 2, the world: you aim at an unsolved prize problem; the proof is longer than 60 seconds of typing, so the minute-you starts leaving it in daily instalments, numbered 1 of 212.
Catch bites: instalment 9 is replaced by errands, 'move out by Friday', 'sell the steno machine'. The minute-you is running your life and you are its hands.
Narrow escape: the landlord note pays off, the eggs pay off (absurd, exact, and funny), proving the minute-you is always right.
Climax choice: tonight's minute can finish the proof instalment that makes you famous, or answer the Maya question; both will not fit in 60 seconds. You choose, and it costs the other.
Callback and twist: the clock hits 0:00, the arm note is new: 'SOMEONE ELSE HAS A MINUTE. HERS STARTS AT 9:00. BE FASTER.'

About 6 min: the notes stop answering you and start ordering you (minute-you has its own plan).
About 9 min: the Maya line turns the power from a tool into a temptation.

topics.title: What If You Could Set Your Life's Difficulty?
topics.premise: What if you had a difficulty slider for your whole life, from 1 to 10, and every reward scaled with it?
topics.world: Seoul, in won, the week of the Suneung, the one-day university exam for which planes are held on the ground: a whole country that sets one day to 'hard', and a slider is strangest there.

thumbnail.image: You lounging in an exam hall with feet on the desk while everyone else sweats; floating beside you a glowing game slider at DIFFICULTY 1; your rival staring at you, pencil snapped.

topics.rule: A slider only you can see, 1 to 10, default 5; one change per day. Lower: lights turn green, questions are ones you know, people say yes. Higher: everything resists. Catch: every reward is multiplied by the setting, pay, respect, even how good the win feels, and level 10 has a lock on it.
topics.hook: It is the hardest exam day in the country and the planes are grounded so nobody is disturbed. You finish in nine minutes, put your feet on the desk, and feel absolutely nothing. A slider beside your head reads DIFFICULTY: 1.
beats: Cold open: feet on the desk, the silent sky, a pigeon landing on your paper and filling in a correct bubble (absurd detail); the win feels like cardboard.
Rules; the readout DIFFICULTY: 5 on a normal day. Baseline against you: half a million students sit this exam after years of 15-hour days. You have a slider.

The fun at 1 and 2: every traffic light green, the crane game gives up its prizes, your crush Seo-yeon says yes before you finish asking. Rewards arrive shrunk: the prize is a keyring, the date is 'fine'.
Jump 1: you try 7. The bus breaks down, the teacher picks on you, the bibimbap is the best thing you have ever tasted, and a B+ feels like a medal. You notice the multiplier.
The promised dilemma: your friend and rival Min-jun has been living at what looks like a 9 his whole life, and he is brilliant. 10 is locked, with a label: REWARD: UNKNOWN.

Jump 2, scheming: you farm it like a game. Slide to 9 for the hours that pay (practice, auditions, the interview), drop to 2 for chores and commutes. Your grades and your reputation go vertical; the slider's daily limit starts to pinch.
Catch: the slider is not private in effect. On your easy days someone near you has a terrible one: Seo-yeon's bus, Min-jun's printer. Difficulty looks conserved.
Jump 3, the big scale: you test it. A whole day at 1 for you; you map every piece of bad luck within a kilometre. The city is paying for your green lights.
The lock opens on exam eve. 10 is available for one day: tomorrow.

Climax choice: Suneung morning. At 1 you pass for certain, it means nothing, and the people around you eat the difficulty. At 10 everything will fight you, the reward is unknown, and the people around you get the easiest exam of their lives. You slide, and it costs you the sure thing.

Callback and twist: nine minutes into the exam the planes are still grounded, the pigeon is back, and your slider moves by itself to 11. Across the hall, Min-jun has his hand on something you cannot see.

topics.title: What If You Spoke Every Language on Earth?
topics.premise: What if you woke up able to speak, read, and write all 7,164 living languages—and every forgotten dead script in history—like a native born on the same street?
topics.world: Present-day Istanbul and Antwerp, from the 4,000-shop Grand Bazaar and Bosphorus shipping lanes to Antwerp's high-security Diamond Quarter, where global fortunes and ancient contraband move across dozens of closed dialects.

thumbnail.image: You at a crowded Istanbul bazaar counter speaking effortlessly with a glowing '7,164 LANGUAGES: 100%' badge beside your head, while three stunned merchants drop their tea glasses.

topics.rule: Whenever anyone speaks or writes near you, your HUD identifies the exact language, regional village dialect, and century ('LANGUAGE #4,812 — PONTIC GREEK: 100%'), and your vocal cords reproduce it with native mother-tongue prosody. Limits: it only works on structured human or historical languages, not random encryption keys. Catch: Linguistic Relativity—speaking any language at 100% native fluency rewires your brain's emotional framing to match that language's worldview while you speak it, and reading an undeciphered dead script aloud immediately exposes you to the people who killed to keep it untranslated.
topics.hook: Two tourists at an Istanbul tram stop whisper in a tiny mountain dialect spoken by only 400 villagers in the Caucasus, laughing at your shoes—and their jaws hit the pavement when you answer them in their grandmother's exact village accent.
beats: Cold open: At the Sultanahmet tram stop, two travelers mock your jacket in Archi—a Caucasian language with 1.5 million verb forms spoken by one village—and your HUD flashes 'LANGUAGE #6,904: 100%' as you reply in flawless Archi, making them drop their bags in shock. So what if you spoke every language on Earth?

Baseline & rules: There are 7,164 living languages on Earth, yet 96% of humanity speaks just 4% of them; overnight, no private conversation in an elevator, restaurant, or diplomatic lounge is ever closed to you.

Jump 1 (The Grand Bazaar & In-Group Discount): In Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, you test the 'In-Group Accent Effect'—switching from English ('$1,200') to Istanbul Turkish ('$600') to the merchant's exact childhood southeastern Mardin Arabic dialect ('$140 and free tea'), flipping rare carpets for a 400% margin by Friday.

Complication: You discover the cognitive side effect—when you speak Guugu Yimithirr, you suddenly know exact compass North blindfolded; when you switch into Russian or Spanish, your risk tolerance and emotional temperature shift with the grammar.

Jump 2 (Antwerp's Diamond Bourse): You fly to Antwerp's Hoveniersstraat, where $180 million a day in rough diamonds is traded without written contracts in a mix of Yiddish, Gujarati, Flemish, and French sealed with 'Mazel u'Bracha'; by catching a side-whisper in Surti Gujarati about a newly discovered Lesotho pink rough stone, you broker a $1.4M cut.

Early dilemma planted: You befriend Dr. Leyla, an epigrapher in Istanbul who has spent 22 years trying to decipher a single clay tablet of Linear A; you can read it at a glance ('MINOAN LINEAR A — 1650 BCE: 100%'), but reading it for her in 5 seconds will either erase her life's work or paint a target on both of you.

Escalation: The Chennai Museum's $1,000,000 public prize to decipher the 4,500-year-old Indus Valley Script tempts you; you anonymously submit a partial phonetic key that passes every computational check, triggering an international sensation.

The trap springs: A private Geneva antiquities billionaire lures you and Leyla onto his Bosphorus yacht to authenticate a looted bronze treaty seal written in an extinct Anatolian script—and as you read the inscription silently, you see it isn't a treaty: it's the exact GPS-equivalent coastal map to a sunken bronze-age royal shipwreck in Turkish waters.

The crisis: The billionaire's armed guards lock the cabin doors; he doesn't want the seal authenticated—he wants the coordinates read aloud so his divers can strip the wreck tonight and sink the witnesses.

Climax choice: You read the bronze seal aloud to the billionaire with fake coordinates pointing straight into a Turkish Coast Guard patrol grid—while slipping a single borrowed idiom in Laz (the Black Sea coastal dialect spoken by the yacht's own helmsman) that warns the helmsman his boss plans to scuttle the crew, turning the crew against the guards in thirty seconds.

Callback & Part 2 twist: Back in Leyla's university office after the Coast Guard secures the wreck, she hands you a photograph of a 15th-century vellum page—the Voynich Manuscript—and as your HUD locks onto the script, it doesn't say 'UNKNOWN': it flashes a location and a date three years in the future.
restarts: Minute 3: Graduating from eavesdropping on tourists to arbitraging Antwerp's multi-lingual diamond bourses.
Minute 7: Discovering that dead, undeciphered scripts (Linear A, Indus Valley) are readable to you—and worth millions.
Minute 11: Trapped on a Bosphorus yacht with a looted map seal, using the yacht helmsman's rare childhood dialect to stage a mutiny.

topics.title: What If Only 100 People Could Ever See You?
topics.premise: What if only 100 people on Earth could see or hear you, and you chose exactly who?
topics.world: Shinjuku, Tokyo, in yen, today: the busiest station on Earth, millions of people a day, is the strangest place to be unseen and the best picture of it.

thumbnail.image: You standing still in a rush-hour crowd that flows around and through your space without a glance; one single person across the concourse staring right at you; a glowing label over your head: 100 / 100.

topics.rule: Exactly 100 living people can see, hear and remember you: your list. Everyone else perceives nothing, even on video. You may swap one name a day. Catch: a removed person loses every memory of you, and the list must always be full.
topics.hook: You are standing in the middle of the busiest train station on Earth, shouting. Three and a half million people will pass you today. A list in your hand says exactly one hundred of them could hear you, and you have used ninety-nine.
beats: Cold open: the shout nobody hears, a salaryman eating an onigiri through the space where your head is (absurd detail), the list with one blank line.
Rules; the readout 99 / 100. Baseline against you: a normal person is known by about 600 people and seen by tens of thousands in a lifetime. You get 100, total.
The fun: unseen by 8.2 billion. Front row at any concert, the cockpit jump seat, the Emperor's garden; automatic doors still open for you, which terrifies a security guard.
Catch 1: you cannot buy a rice ball. No cashier sees you; no doctor, no barber, no bus driver stops. Being served needs a slot.
Jump 1, scheming: slots become your currency. You add a ramen cook, a dentist, a landlord. Family and friends are getting squeezed: 100 fills up brutally fast.
The promised dilemma: your grandmother holds slot 1. She has no idea she is on a list.

Jump 2, status: you redraw the list for power. A minister, a billionaire, a news anchor, the country's top idol. To the 100 most powerful people in Japan you are the voice only they can hear. They start doing what you say.
Catch 2: every friend you swapped out now walks past you in Shinjuku like the salaryman did. One of them is your best friend Kenji, eating an onigiri.
Jump 3, the strange discovery: a girl on the Yamanote platform looks straight at you. She is not on your list. You check twice.

Climax choice: Kenji is in real trouble only a specific lawyer could fix, the lawyer needs a slot today, and the only slot whose loss would not collapse your new empire is slot 1. Empire, friend, or grandmother: one of them forgets you tonight.

Callback and twist: you are shouting in Shinjuku again, and this time one person turns. The girl. She holds up her own list. You are number 100 on it, added this morning, and she is about to make her daily swap.
restarts: About 3 min: freedom flips to 'I can't buy lunch'.
About 6 min: the list as a power tool (the 100 most powerful).
About 9 min: someone off-list sees you.
End: you are on someone else's list.

topics.title: What If You Took 1 Second From Everyone Alive?
topics.premise: What if you could take one second from every person on Earth and keep all 8.2 billion of them for yourself?
topics.world: Biel/Bienne, the Swiss watch town, in francs, today: you are a watch-repair apprentice, the prop is a pocket watch with one pusher, and everyone around you measures seconds for a living.

thumbnail.image: You holding a glowing pocket watch in a street where every person is frozen mid-blink; over the watch a label reads 259 YEARS; one frozen man's coffee hangs in the air.

topics.rule: Press the pusher: every living human skips the same single second and never notices. You bank all of them, about 260 years, to spend as time in which only you move, and you don't age while spending it. One press a day. Catch: the world's machines do not skip, and whatever each person was doing in that second happens without them.
topics.hook: You press a button on a broken pocket watch. Across the planet, 8.2 billion people blink at once. The dial now says you own 259 years, 10 months, and the soup you were carrying is still in the air.
beats: Cold open: the soup in the air (absurd detail), the master watchmaker frozen mid-sneeze, the dial reading 259 Y 10 M.
Rules; the baseline against you: a human life is about 73 years, so one press just handed you three and a half lifetimes of free time.
The fun: you spend 'an afternoon' of frozen time fixing every watch in the shop, learning the trade, rearranging the town square for a laugh. The dial barely moves: 259 Y 10 M.
Jump 1, status: the apprentice who repairs anything overnight. A collector brings a watch nobody could fix in 40 years; you take two frozen years over it, and hand it back 'the next morning'.
The promised dilemma: your friend Noé, a goalkeeper, lets in a goal at the exact second of your second press and cannot explain where he went. The second came from somewhere.
You do the maths on a napkin: one press costs humanity 260 years of living, spread so thin nobody feels it. Is a theft real if no victim can notice?

Catch: machines kept running. The news that week: a strange one-second 'stumble' in typing logs, game replays, heart monitors, every human on Earth late by exactly one second against their own clocks. Scientists start hunting the cause.

Jump 2: you spend decades frozen: read the town library, walk to Paris and back between two ticks, become someone much older inside than outside. Lonely, magnificent montage with one clear action per shot.
Jump 3: the stumble-hunters triangulate. Everything on Earth skipped except one person's keystrokes. Yours.

topics.premise: What if every object, meal, and handshake had a glowing tag showing the exact money it will make or cost you ten years from today?
topics.world: Present-day London, moving from Brick Lane charity shops to Lloyd's of London and Mayfair private auctions, where centuries-old junk sits beside billion-dollar financial liabilities.

thumbnail.image: You holding a battered $5 wristwatch at a street stall while a glowing green '+$1,400,000' floats above it, as a wealthy dealer beside you reaches for a luxury briefcase glowing red '-$3,200,000'.

topics.rule: Whenever you look at an object, contract, or handshake, an in-world readout shows your exact net 10-year financial gain or loss in dollars if you take it right now. Limits: you only see the final 10-year net number, never the chain of events that causes it. Catch: every choice you make immediately recalculates every other tag around you, and the tag only measures your own bank balance—never the non-financial cost to the people you love.
topics.hook: You're about to drink a free $3 energy can at a London train station when a glowing red tag hovers over the pull-tab reading '-$18,400'—the exact cost of the kidney stone and missed flight it triggers six years from tonight.
beats: Cold open: At Liverpool Street Station, a free energy drink flashes '-$18,400' while a damp $2 umbrella in the lost-and-found bin glows '+$64,000'; you buy the umbrella, share it in a downpour with a soaked stranger, and land a private courier job by noon. Baseline & rules: You test the readout across your apartment—your cheap office chair reads '-$29,000' in future spinal surgery, while a $40 smoke detector reads '+$310,000'; the rules lock in: three tags max in view, net 10-year personal cash impact only, no explanation why.

Jump 1 (Street arbitrage): You scour Portobello Road and Brick Lane charity shops, skipping fake antiques showing '-$400' until a box of 1970s technical manuals glows '+$480,000' because an unpatented chemical seal inside is still unassigned.

topics.premise: What if every time you missed a shot, slipped a millimeter, or mistimed a move, your nervous system permanently deleted that error so you could never make it again?

content_mine.fact: Even the greatest free-throw shooter in NBA history, Stephen Curry (91.0% career accuracy), misses roughly 9 out of every 100 attempts due to neuromotor noise in the motor cortex.
content_mine.beat: The trap springs: why never missing again is a curse when you need to prove you're human.

topics.twist: Once your brain deletes an error, you physically CANNOT miss on purpose even to save yourself from being flagged as a machine—and the only way to save someone's life in surgery is to intentionally fail six times on a test rig in 90 seconds.
topics.ending: You'll never feel embarrassed about failing on your first try the same way once you realize every mistake is just your nervous system crossing off where the target isn't.
